title: Taking good notes
examples: Teacher, how do I know which notes to keep?
Is mind mapping better than writing notes?
What is the best way to review my notes later?

explain.say: Today we will learn three great ways to take good notes. These methods help you remember what you learn.

items: Summary: Overall summary at the bottom

explain.say: The Cornell method divides your page into sections. You write main ideas in the large section. Then you write keywords in the narrow column.

draw.text: Cornell Notes: Divide page into three sections.

explain.say: Next we will look at mind maps for organizing thoughts. You put the main topic in the center circle. Then you draw branches out for related ideas.

draw.text: Mind Maps: Central topic, branching ideas.

explain.say: Mind maps show how ideas connect visually. For example, if the topic is planets, you branch out to Mars and Jupiter. You draw lines to show links.
Finally, summarising means writing a short overview. You take all your notes and write the main point in just a few sentences. This helps you review quickly.

draw.text: Summarising: Main idea in few sentences.

explain.say: In real life, you can use these skills when reading a textbook chapter. First, use Cornell notes to capture details. Then, make a mind map of the chapter's themes. Finally, write a summary paragraph at the end.

draw.text: Study Skills: Combine methods for review.

faq.q: Should I write everything the teacher says in my notes?
faq.a: No, you should not write everything. Focus on the main ideas and key vocabulary words. You might also ask, 'What is the best amount of detail to write down?' or 'Should I write down every example?'
asks: Do I need to write everything?

faq.q: Are mind maps good for all subjects?
faq.a: Mind maps work well for subjects with many related ideas, like history or science. They help you see connections between topics. You could also ask, 'Can I use this for maths?' or 'Is this only for art?'
asks: Are mind maps only for certain subjects?

faq.q: How long should my summary be?
faq.a: Your summary should be short, usually just a few sentences. It needs to capture the overall meaning, not just list facts. You might ask, 'How many sentences is enough?' or 'Should the summary be long?'
asks: What is the length of a good summary?
How detailed should the summary be?

faq.q: What is the difference between notes and a summary?
faq.a: Notes are detailed records of what was taught. A summary is your own short explanation of the most important points. Think of notes as raw material and the summary as the finished product. You could ask, 'Are they the same thing?' or 'Do I write the summary first?'
asks: When do I write the summary?

faq.q: What if the teacher moves quickly?
faq.a: If the teacher moves fast, it is okay to write down bullet points or just the main keywords. You can always ask a classmate to repeat the key points later. You could also ask, 'What if I miss something?' or 'Can I record the lesson?'
asks: What to do when the pace is fast?
If I fall behind in notes?

facts: Cornell notes use three distinct sections for organization.
Mind maps use branches to show relationships between ideas.
Summarising requires rewriting information in your own words.
Keywords help you recall the main concepts later.

quiz.say: Which method uses a central topic with radiating branches?
quiz.show: Mind Maps: Central topic, radiating branches.
quiz.why: Mind maps are designed specifically to show connections radiating from one central idea.

wrong.0: Cornell notes use distinct, separated sections, not radiating branches.
wrong.1: Summarising is the act of writing a short overview, not a visual structure.
wrong.2: A timeline shows events in order over time, which is different from idea connections.

quiz.say: If you are reviewing notes, what is the best first step to recall details?

options.show: Covering the notes and using keywords
options.say: Covering the notes and using keywords

quiz.why: Using the cues column forces your brain to actively recall the information, which is better for memory.

wrong.0: Headings are too general; you need the specific keywords to prompt memory.
wrong.2: Reading only the summary is passive and does not test your memory recall.
wrong.3: Rewriting is time-consuming and less effective than active recall using keywords.

quiz.say: When creating a summary, what should you focus on?

options.show: The main idea in a few sentences
options.say: The main idea in a few sentences

options.show: Copying full sentences from the textbook
options.say: Copying full sentences from the textbook

quiz.why: The goal of summarising is to condense the core message into your own concise language.

wrong.1: Copying full sentences is plagiarism and does not show you understand the concept.
wrong.2: Listing every fact makes it too long and loses the overall main point.
wrong.3: Keywords are prompts; the summary needs to explain what those keywords mean together.
